questions.stem: A patient on dialysis must attend hospital three times per week for 4-hour sessions. During dialysis, their blood flows past a partially permeable membrane with dialysis fluid on the other side. Why does the dialysis fluid contain normal blood glucose concentration but no urea?

options.text: To add extra glucose to the patient's blood and remove water
To maintain the glucose concentration gradient at zero (preventing glucose loss) while maintaining a steep urea gradient to remove urea from the blood
Because urea would damage the dialysis machine
Because glucose is a waste product that needs to be added back

questions.explanation: The dialysis fluid is carefully designed: it contains normal glucose levels so there is no net movement of glucose out of the blood. It contains no urea, creating a steep concentration gradient that allows urea to diffuse from the blood (high concentration) across the membrane into the dialysis fluid (low concentration).

questions.stem: A patient receives a kidney transplant from a donor. Why must the patient take immunosuppressant drugs for the rest of their life?

options.text: To prevent the transplanted kidney from producing too much urine
To prevent the patient's immune system from recognising the donor kidney as foreign and attacking it
To keep the donor kidney alive outside the body
To prevent the patient from developing diabetes

questions.explanation: The donor kidney has different surface antigens (proteins) on its cells. The patient's immune system would recognise these as foreign and mount an immune response (rejection), destroying the transplanted kidney. Immunosuppressants reduce this immune response, but also make the patient more vulnerable to infections.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure must restrict their protein intake while awaiting treatment. Why is this dietary restriction important?

options.text: Protein causes high blood sugar levels
Excess protein is broken down to form urea, which the failing kidneys cannot adequately remove
Protein blocks the remaining nephrons
Protein increases blood volume, putting pressure on the kidneys

questions.explanation: When proteins are broken down, the amino group is removed (deamination) and converted to urea in the liver. If the kidneys cannot filter urea effectively, it builds up in the blood to toxic levels. Reducing protein intake reduces urea production, helping manage the condition.

questions.stem: Comparing dialysis and kidney transplant as treatments for kidney failure, which is a key advantage of a transplant over long-term dialysis?

options.text: A transplant requires no medical follow-up after surgery
A successful transplant provides continuous filtration and frees the patient from regular dialysis sessions
A transplant eliminates the need for any medication
A transplant is always available immediately when needed

questions.explanation: A functioning transplanted kidney works continuously, filtering blood 24/7 like a healthy kidney. This frees the patient from spending several hours multiple times per week connected to a dialysis machine, greatly improving quality of life. However, they still need immunosuppressant medication.

questions.stem: During haemodialysis, the blood and dialysis fluid flow in opposite directions (counter-current flow). Why is this arrangement more effective than flowing in the same direction?

options.text: It prevents blood clots from forming in the machine
It maintains a concentration gradient along the entire length of the membrane, maximising the removal of waste
It makes the blood flow faster, reducing treatment time
It warms the blood to body temperature more efficiently

questions.explanation: Counter-current flow ensures that blood always meets dialysis fluid with a lower concentration of waste products. This maintains a concentration gradient along the entire length of the membrane, ensuring more efficient diffusion of urea and other wastes out of the blood.
